title: The Vasa Sinks on Its Maiden Voyage
text:
In the 1620s King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden, at war in the Baltic, ordered a great new warship for his navy. The Vasa was built in Stockholm under the Dutch shipwright Henrik Hybertsson, who died before it was finished. The king followed the work closely and approved its size and armament. It was given two full gun decks with heavy cannon, an unusual and ambitious design, and was richly decorated with carved sculptures.

Before it sailed, Admiral Klas Fleming had a stability test carried out: thirty men ran back and forth across the deck together. After three runs the ship was rolling so heavily that the test was stopped. Nobody, it seems, knew how to fix the problem, and the king, away at war, was pressing for the ship to be ready. The test results did not stop the launch.

On 10 August 1628 the Vasa set sail from Stockholm harbor in front of crowds. After sailing about 1,300 meters, a gust of wind heeled it over. Water poured in through the open lower gunports, and the ship sank in minutes. Some thirty people died.

An inquiry was held. The captain, the crew and the builders were questioned, and each testified that they had followed instructions. In the end no one was punished. In 1961 the remarkably preserved ship was raised, and it is now one of Sweden's most visited museums.
lesson: When everyone sees a problem but no one feels able to stop the project, the whole team fails together. Make it safe to halt a launch when a test goes wrong.
people: Gustavus Adolphus, Henrik Hybertsson, Klas Fleming
source: Records of the 1628 inquiry; Vasa Museum research publications, e.g. Fred Hocker, Vasa (2011)
